posts.cooked:
I want to respond to the concerns raised in connection with A272 and clarify my position.

Astroport and Estima

My position was that the Foundation should assess the available options before committing substantial funding to a new DEX. That included comparing maintenance, a fork or a handover of existing infrastructure against new development, including costs, security and long-term maintenance.

I also suggested seeking proposals from other developers and involving Terra governance where the decision had significant implications for the wider ecosystem.

I sought clarification from Astroport’s team about its governance arrangements and received reassurance. My objections to the proposed alternative concerned concentration of control, audit requirements and access to source code.

During the incident, I voted on and executed the Astroport liquidity withdrawal, LA A34.

Before the incident, I had expressed support for the DEX subject to governance, admin-control and source-access safeguards. I subsequently voted for and executed the revised Estima grant, A266.

DeFi and ecosystem development

I support developing DeFi on Terra. My suggestion to get LUNA listed on launchpad platforms alongside meme coins was intended to attract users and trading volume, not to turn Terra into a meme coin.

My concerns about DeFi proposals have focused on oracle reliability, liquidation mechanisms, block capacity, source-code access and concentration of control. Raising those concerns is not opposition to DeFi development.

Grants and funding

I support the Foundation’s mandate to fund ecosystem development. By saying grants should be the exception, I meant approval should not be auto-default approval. Each application needs due diligence, clear deliverables and consideration of alternatives.

The community entrusted PF with assessing and approving funding. I also believe major, long-term commitments may warrant broader community discussion or a Terra governance vote. That does not mean every funding decision needs to go to governance.

Board governance and accountability

Directors should exercise independent judgment and question proposals. Disagreement alone is not misconduct.

I support an independent review of the relevant conduct of all four directors, including my own, using the same standards and giving each an opportunity to present evidence and respond.

I favour stronger independent oversight and adding independent directors while keeping the Board small and effective.

PF should remain accountable to the Terra community. Any governance changes should be transparent and follow the applicable procedures.

As a PF Director, I can attest that your account omits critical internal information and context.

An independent review with access to the Foundation’s internal records is necessary to verify these statements and establish a complete, unbiased account of the events.

posts.cooked:
Honestly at this point, (and if the accused has no issue with it of course) just share it… it’s going to be made public anyway. Why drag it out and further dramatize the process?

Edit (to avoid double-commenting): I meant to reply to the comment just above mine originally, but this is in addition to Vini’s comment, and touches on some important and constructive points.

Cosmwasm (and therefore Astroport to a large degree) have been covered by a very healthy bug bounty program for many years now, thanks to the Sei team (whether they like it or not).
They have paid out over $10m in bounties, which over the past 2 years or so have tapered off to essentially nothing.

Statistics show the majority of inceidents do not involve very new workers, or very seasoned workers. Overwhelmingly they involve workers who are in a sort of cursed spot in their career, which is around 10,000 hours in their current role, or a very similar role.
For whatever reason this is about the time where people often become “comfortable” in their position, typically having worked until that point wihtout any major incident occurring on their watch.
This is not a fault of that person, it’s a literal trait of being human. It can happen to anyone, in any position, and it happens across all industried.

Having been in the work force for over 30 years, and through multiple experiences incljding my own, (which could very easily have been fatal, had there not been other safety procedures in place), in any serious (damage/loss-causing) incident or near-miss (which the recent astroport which had the potential for a large amount of loss is technically classified as), the person deemed “at fault” for it is almost never removed from their position becasue of it.
They are usually pulled into a formal process where they investigate the hell out of whatever happened, then discuss it openly with the team and anyone else who was involved. Everyone takes part in this process, they all learn and benefit from that person’s experience (instead of by making a similar mistake at some point), and they move on.

If they are let go following an incident, it’s due to a clear inability or the unwillingness to learn from it. If they respect the depth of the situation (and most do), that person is now the ideal person for that position, as they will be extremely vigilant from that point on, doing everything within their power to ensure nothing like that ever happens again.

vini:

I sought clarification from Astroport’s team about its governance arrangements and received reassurance

As another director I can confirm that this is not at all the full account and the post either misrepresents or is quite inaccurate.

There are large and serious intractable issues existing.

This is why an Emergency Supervisor has been requested to resolve this with the directors directly.

At this point, I think it is clear that the Foundation cannot continue operating as it currently does. However, the proposed solution of removing one director and effectively concentrating power in the hands of the remaining two seems far more dangerous, not only for the community but also for the directors themselves.

Regarding Philip’s proposal to appoint an emergency supervisor to help resolve the internal dispute, I agree that, if no better alternative is available, external supervision may be the most practical way forward. However, I would prefer to wait for the response from the permanent supervisor that Rose is in contact with before making a final decision.

If that option is not viable, then I believe an emergency supervisor must be someone demonstrably independent and impartial.

For that reason, I do not believe the directors should have a role in nominating or selecting the supervisor. Given the current dispute, allowing the directors to influence the appointment risks creating a perception of bias, regardless of the individual’s actual intentions.

If emergency supervision is the only realistic way to protect the Foundation and restore confidence in its governance, the appointment process must be beyond reasonable doubt. The position should be opened to independent candidates, either through an open call for applications or through voluntary candidatures, under clearly defined and publicly agreed conditions.

I also think we should acknowledge that much of the information surrounding this dispute is internal and unavailable to the wider community. Therefore, arguing in favour of one individual or against another based on incomplete information is unlikely to help us reach a fair outcome.

For these reasons, I cannot support the current proposal as it stands, given that the proposed supervisor was nominated by the directors involved in the dispute. Unless all directors explicitly agree in writing to the nomination and the proposed appointment process, I believe we need a new proposal.

My suggestion is to establish a transparent process that clearly defines the supervisor’s independence, eligibility criteria, responsibilities, authority, limitations, rights, and expected duration of the appointment. It should also explain how candidates can put themselves forward and how the final appointment will be decided.

The objective should not be to help one side prevail over the other. It should be to protect the Foundation, community,Terra and the directors themselves through a process that everyone can reasonably regard as fair and independent.

Without that transparency, even a well-intentioned appointment risks deepening the existing divisions rather than resolving them.

Applications were open, and every Director has had since 5 October to propose candidates. No other qualified candidate came forward.

MB and I support Martin for his legal background and non-involvement in general drama. Neither Vini (Phoenix Foundation: Appointment of an Emergency Supervisor - #29 by vini) nor Rose (Phoenix Foundation: Appointment of an Emergency Supervisor - #31 by rose) has ruled him out publicly and are okay with him. Martin will be required to provide an independence declaration with his acceptance.

Requiring unanimous approval creates a veto the Bylaws do not provide. Lets not continue derailing the discussion and prolonging the issue.

The proposal goes to Terra Governance tomorrow. The community decides.

Before validators vote, the “community” should see who decides where their voting power comes from.

image2400×940 265 KB

The numbers (Terra block 23,401,494, 22 October, 11:08 UTC)

41.3% of Terra’s voting power, 126.5M of 306.4M LUNA, is staked with validators either by Stewardship DAO votes or by ERIS.

  • 30.9% is VT staked through the Alliance module by the Phoenix treasury (11.1%) and four TLA connector contracts (19.8%). All five stake the same 25 validators in identical proportions. Stewardship proposals A4 to A6, A20 and A21 placed it, and 12 redelegation proposals since (A61 to A218) moved it. Philipp proposed all 17. Each passed with three or four Director votes, and every Director voted for some of them.
  • 10.4% is the stake behind ampLUNA, which follows ERIS’s vAMP gauge. ERIS’s docs list Philipp as CEO. About 65% of all ampLUNA is held, directly or through pool shares, by the community’s liquidity multisig, funded with 30M LUNA by proposal 4844. Most of the stake ERIS directs is the community’s own LUNA.

For comparison, quorum is 30% of voting power and the veto threshold is 33.4% of votes cast. Rose has pointed to Terra’s Nakamoto coefficient of 7 (topic 33). That counts validators. Counted by who decides where stake goes, the Stewardship alone places 30.9%, and with ERIS 41.3%.

image2400×2176 450 KB

Who depends on it

  • 25 validators hold Stewardship VT or ERIS ampLUNA stake. For 21 of them it is more than half their voting power, and those 21 hold 47.7% of all voting power. They include five of the ten largest validators, among them the largest, Smart Stake (69%).
  • Two of the 25 are linked to Directors: ERIS, whose operator key is the wallet Philipp lists as his own (99% of its power from these sources), and SCV-Security, Vini’s company (84%). I found no validator linked to Rose or MB.

Why it matters for this vote

The Directive makes validators the final check on it: “Terra stakers and validators have the ultimate decision or veto power” (topic 45). Yet the Stewardship decides where almost a third of the stake those validators vote with sits, and ERIS another tenth.

That is a structural conflict of interest, whatever anyone intends.

I’m not alleging any threat or inducement. But for those 21, a no vote is weighed against the stake behind most of their voting power and commission. The same applies to Vini’s validator as to Philipp’s.

About 9.8% of the VT table still sits with two validators that are jailed and unbonded. Concerning on it’s own for lack of management.

This proposal should fail in it’s current form and should be posted on chain with a remit to review the adherence to the bylaws and actions of all Directors.

posts.cooked:
Yes. On the public record there’s a solid conflict-of-interest case, and the clearest way to frame it is by the Foundation’s own rules, because A272 uses those same rules against Vini. Here’s the case, separating what Philipp has confirmed himself from what critics have shown but he hasn’t addressed.

The standard being applied

Article 4.6.2 says a person aware of an ongoing material conflict must resign unless it’s disclosed to the Board and Community and approved by a majority of disinterested Directors. Article 3.2.5.3 requires each member to vote on proposals without regard to any personal interest. A272 accused Vini of breaching exactly this: it attacks him over A249, a grant that paid his own company despite a recognized conflict. So the question is whether Philipp meets the standard he’s prosecuting Vini under. phoenixphoenix

1. Voting on payments to himself

Rarma documented Philipp voting yes on five milestone releases, 305,000 USDC in total, paid to the wallet Philipp lists as his own in topic 10, each passing with exactly three votes. That means his vote was necessary for each to pass. Rarma found no 4.6.2 disclosure or recusal record for these releases. Separately, MaxP counted at least seven proposals Philipp authored and voted for that paid his own address, totalling $20,450 and 3,500 LUNA, with no on-chain record of disclosure or disinterested-director approval. Phoenix Foundation: Appointment of an Emergency Supervisor +2

His defense is that milestone payments are tied to contractual deliverables, other directors do the verification, and the release is a formality. The weakness is obvious: if it’s a formality, he could have abstained, and with exactly three yes votes each time, his abstention would have changed the outcome. phoenix

2. ERIS, ampLUNA and the 30M LUNA

Proposal 4844 is verifiable on-chain: it requested 30M LUNA from the community pool to deploy liquidity into USDC–ampLUNA and LUNA–ampLUNA pools on Astroport. Rarma’s charge is that ERIS, which lists Philipp as CEO, takes 8% of ampLUNA staking rewards, the draft was put on-chain by ERIS’s owner address, and the draft didn’t mention his ERIS role or that fee. If accurate, a director steered 30M LUNA of community funds into a product his own company earns fees from, without disclosing it. That’s a textbook conflict. To be fair, Terra governance did approve 4844, so the issue is disclosure, not authorization. Philipp has not responded to this point in the thread. valopersphoenix

3. Retaining control he promised to hand over

This is the one he’s essentially admitted. His August 2024 TLA proposal said contract admin would go to PD Stewardship after one month and ownership after three. Ex_TFL cited transactions showing that, among other things, in October 2025 a Philipp-controlled wallet changed the registry’s fee recipient from the board to the Eris fee account. Philipp’s reply: ERIS still administers the TLA contracts because it develops and maintains them, and given his concerns about the board, ERIS hasn’t considered transferring that authority appropriate. So his company holds admin power over Foundation infrastructure, a fee flow was redirected to his company, and the handover was withheld based on his personal view of the board that’s supposed to oversee him. Ex_TFL repeatedly asked who approved departing from the published terms, under what authority and when, and that was never answered. Phoenix Foundation: Appointment of an Emergency Supervisor +3

4. Influence over the validators who will decide this vote

Rarma’s on-chain analysis shows 41.3% of Terra’s voting power is staked with validators either by Stewardship DAO votes or by ERIS, and Philipp proposed all 17 Stewardship proposals that placed or moved the Alliance stake. ERIS’s own validator, whose operator key is Philipp’s listed wallet, gets 99% of its power from these sources. Rarma explicitly isn’t alleging inducement, but the validators voting on Philipp’s proposal depend on stake that Philipp directs. Phoenix Foundation: Appointment of an Emergency Supervisor +2

5. A process shaped to his advantage

A272 paired removal with a threshold cut to 60%, and MB has voted identically to Philipp on all 119 proposals where both voted. The standing Supervisor is in office, but A272 wasn’t referred to them because Philipp says that wasn’t required and they can’t instruct removal. When asked to put all four directors under equal review, he said no, calling it an open-ended investigation that would derail the process. And Ex_TFL claims both proposed supervisors were contacted in advance by Philipp, which hasn’t been confirmed or denied. Phoenix Foundation: Appointment of an Emergency Supervisor +3

Bottom line

Yes, on its face Philipp has multiple material conflicts: payments to his own wallet that his vote was needed to pass, an undisclosed fee interest in a 30M LUNA community deployment, retained administrative control over Foundation infrastructure, and influence over the stake behind the validators deciding his proposal. Whether these are formal breaches depends on whether 4.6.2 disclosures and disinterested-director approvals exist somewhere, and no one has produced them. The strongest single argument is the double standard: the conflict rule he invoked to remove Vini, applied evenly, catches him at least as squarely.
